new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-distinctive. Prominence (stress and pitch) falls on the first complex vowel (long vowel or diphthong) of the word if there is one; in words without complex vowels it falls on the initial syllable. The initial syllable is the prosodically dominant position (also shown by vowel harmony and sandhi).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the visible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: None visible in the snippets; 'tends to' and 'normally' hedge the rule. Janhunen 1990 (p. 32) adds that within closing diphthongs the main stress lies on the first component in an open syllable and on the second in a closed syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('word stress'); non-distinctive. Janhunen's 1990/2005 descriptions are based on Manchurian (Hulun Buir, China) Khamnigan Mongol. The statement was seen only in Google Books snippets, consistently across four independent queries, not on an opened page.
new_statements.identity_note: kham1281 covers three dialect areas with no separate glottocodes: Manchurian (Hulun Buir, China; Janhunen 1990, 2005 — the source of the stress statement), Onon/Siberian (Russia; Damdinov, Gruntov 2005) and Mongolian (Dadal Sum, Khentii; Uray-Kőhalmi 1959, Yu 2011, Gruntov & Mazo 2022). The stress rule quoted is Janhunen's, based on Manchurian Khamnigan Mongol (Mergel); Gruntov 2005 (Onon dialect) and Uray-Kőhalmi 1959 (Dadal Sum) give no placement statement. All are Mongolic Khamnigan; do not confuse with Khamnigan Evenki (Tungusic), for which Google Books snippets report a different (weight/penult) pattern (Tsumagari 1992).

tone.quote: In the phonological system of Khamnigan that we witnessed in Mongolia 2019 there are many innovations mainly, but not exclusively, due to heavy interaction with Khalkha and to less extent with Buriad, although many archaic features are definitely preserved. We would not present here a general description of Khamnigan phonetics and phonology, referring the reader to Yu Wonsoo (2011: 17-34) and K. U.-Kőhalmi (1959: 165-171).
